issues.claim: scientists think your brain first guesses the light, then subtracts it
issues.problem: Wikipedia notes there is no scientific consensus on the cause, and the paper frames it as a hypothesis. 'First...then' implies a fixed two-step sequence the sources do not describe.
issues.fix: Your eyes don't just record colour; one leading idea is that your brain guesses the light, then discounts it.

issues.claim: Guess cool daylight, and you see white and gold.
issues.problem: Paper says 'cool illuminant'; Conway links it to discounting the blue of daylight. This is a hypothesis presented as fact.
issues.fix: Assume cool, bluish daylight, and you tend to see white and gold.

issues.problem: Paper says 1,401; Wikipedia says about 1,400. Percentages 57/30 confirmed by Wikipedia (independent of the paper); the paper PDF itself could not be parsed by WebFetch, so its quotes in SOURCES.md were not re-checked by me.
issues.fix: In one survey of about 1,400 people, 57 percent saw blue and black, and 30 percent saw white and gold.
